title: Characterizing Full Nonequilibrium Dynamics of Simple Exclusion Processes
authors: Zhimao Liu, Jing Liu, Pan Zhang, Ying Tang
abstract: The simple exclusion process (SEP) is a paradigmatic model for nonequilibrium transport, yet the rich dynamics of its time-dependent joint distribution over an exponentially large configuration space remain notoriously intractable. Here, we leverage variational autoregressive networks to systematically characterize the nonequilibrium dynamics of symmetric (SSEP), asymmetric (ASEP), and totally asymmetric (TASEP) cases from one to three dimensions. We first validate the approach by reproducing the previous finite-time results for the 1D SSEP and long-time tensor-network results for the 2D SSEP, and then provide richer finite-time dynamics of the SSEP, ASEP, and TASEP in 1D and 2D, and a new finite-time analysis in 3D. Specifically, in 1D, we reveal that finite-time dynamical-activity maps directly correspond to the classical three-phase TASEP steady-state organization, and, in the long-time limit, boundary and bulk effects separately govern the dynamical susceptibility during the crossover from diffusive to ballistic transport. In 2D, we establish a mean-field directional-density criterion, supported by our neural-network calculations, and show that long-time boundary and bulk effects mirror their 1D counterparts. In 3D, we uncover new finite-time scaling relations for the active-inactive phase transition of the SSEP, and reveal a broadly consistent scaling exponent of the phase-transition point versus system size, implying that the phase-transition point is asymptotically controlled by the characteristic length scale ($s_c\sim L^{-2}$) regardless of dimension. This work thus establishes a unified framework for characterizing the nonequilibrium dynamics of representative transport systems.
summary: This work develops a novel, unified framework using variational neural networks to simulate and characterize the complex, time-dependent dynamics of Simple Exclusion Processes (SEP) in multiple dimensions. By calculating key quantities like the SCGF, the authors provide detailed insights into phase transitions and transport regimes, establishing a powerful computational tool for nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.
main_problem: The paper tackles the notoriously difficult problem of characterizing the full, time-dependent joint distribution for Simple Exclusion Processes (SEP) in nonequilibrium settings.
main_result: The authors establish a unified framework using variational neural networks to characterize finite-time dynamics across 1D, 2D, and 3D, revealing dimension-independent scaling laws for phase transitions.
method: They employ Variational Autoregressive Networks (VAN) to approximate the evolution of the system's probability distribution governed by a master equation, calculating the Scaled Cumulant Generating Function (SCGF).
model_or_system: The primary model is the Simple Exclusion Process (SEP), including variants like SSEP, ASEP, and TASEP, studied on lattices of increasing dimensions (1D to 3D).
key_observables: Dynamical activity, dynamical susceptibility, time-dependent joint distribution, and the SCGF ($\psi_t(s)$).
important_parameters: System size ($L$), time ($t$), and the counting field ($s$) conjugate to the dynamical observable.
main_assumptions: The core approximation is using the Variational Autoregressive Network (VAN) ansatz to manage the exponentially large configuration space.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the unified framework, showing the master equation under a tilted generator and the pipeline for calculating the variational free energy, alongside comparisons of finite-time vs. steady-state results in 3D.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the intractable problem, details the variational framework using VANs, validates the approach against known results (1D TASEP, 2D SSEP), and then presents dimension-specific findings (1D, 2D, 3D) to establish the unified theory.
why_interesting: The application of advanced machine learning techniques (VANs) to solve fundamental, analytically intractable problems in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics provides a powerful computational tool for studying complex many-body dynamics.
